Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.
Why is a voter-backed initiative required rather than a legislative statute?
We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.

Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.

Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.

Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.

Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

Proposition 39
PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts. It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions to put it on the ballot.
California’s elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in person, and match every mail ballot signature.
A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a driver’s license or Social Security number.
Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name, address, and signature.
Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote again.
An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on them.
A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation, childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage, and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned away anyway.
Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them from voter rolls.
Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay, and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to spread lies.
Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards, audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don’t let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.

Proposition 38
Bonds for Research on the Immune System
Initiative Statute
A newly proposed law placed on the ballot by people who collected enough signatures
The Question
Should California authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research at California research institutions?
The Situation
Medical research in the United States is funded by a combination of private industry, the federal government, universities, and nonprofit organizations. Private industry provides most research funding, while federal agencies such as the National Institutes of Health support a large share of basic scientific research. State governments generally play a smaller role in funding medical research.
Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system. Immunotherapy involves treatments that help the immune system prevent, treat, or cure disease. Researchers are studying immunotherapy as a treatment for cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, heart disease, autoimmune disorders, and other conditions.
California voters have previously approved state bonds for stem cell research. Proposition 71 (2004) authorized $3 billion in bonds, and Proposition 14 (2020) authorized an additional $5.5 billion. Those measures funded research through competitive grant programs.
The Proposal
Voters signed petitions to place Proposition 38 on the ballot. Prop 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion by issuing general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. The bonds would be repaid from the state’s General Fund.
The measure would allocate:
Approximately $4.2 billion to a single nonprofit medical research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health. The institute must meet specific eligibility requirements, including an affiliation with a University of California campus.
Approximately $4.2 billion in competitive grants to California public universities, nonprofit universities, and nonprofit research institutions.
At least half of all funding must support research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.
Universities and institutes that receive grants must buy at least half their goods and services from California suppliers when possible.
The measure would require recipients to return 10% of licensing or revenue generated from funded research to the state. Treatments developed through the program would generally be sold in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The measure also creates oversight committees, reporting requirements, independent audits, and limits state administrative costs to 2% of total bond funding.
Fiscal Effects
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state would pay approximately $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the bonds. Repayment would come from the state’s General Fund.
The state could recover some of these costs if funded research produces discoveries that generate licensing or revenue. The amount and timing of any repayment are uncertain and could take many years.
The measure could also have indirect effects on state health care costs and California’s biotechnology economy, but those impacts are difficult to predict.
Supporters Say
Research funded by Prop 38 could lead to new treatments or cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, heart disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other serious illnesses.
The measure would provide a stable source of funding for California research institutions at a time when federal research funding is uncertain.
Any treatments developed with program funding would generally be sold in California at discounted prices.
The measure includes audits, public reporting, and revenue-sharing requirements intended to protect taxpayers.
Opponents Say
Research outcomes are uncertain. Opponents say the state should not borrow billions of dollars for projects that may never produce new treatments.
Medical research priorities should be set by public health needs and scientific review, not through ballot measures.
Future health needs may change, and opponents say the state should not commit billions of dollars to one area of research for many years.
Half of the funding would go to one research institute instead of being distributed more broadly among California research organizations.

On the ballot this November, Californians will decide if they want the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support research that aims to deliver cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease “in our lifetime.”
Backers say (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) that Proposition 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases and provide a steady funding source amid uncertainty of federal grants. The measure ensures “strong accountability, including independent audits,” and mandates a 20% discount to California residents for treatments developed from this funding.
But critics view the legislation as a Trojan horse: while promising transformative medical breakthroughs, it will channel billions in state funding to a newly created institute that currently has no scientists or researchers.
If Proposition 38 passes, San Diego stands to be a major beneficiary.
The La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Salk Institute, Sanford Burnham Prebys, UC San Diego and Scripps Research — some of the most prominent immunology research institutions in the nation — would likely be on an advisory committee overseeing $4.2 billion, about half of the bond revenue the proposition would generate.
Despite their potential financial stake in its passage, each organization has declined to speak about the measure.
What Proposition 38 says
A “yes” vote would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research for diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
The funding will primarily target early-stage research. In theory, intellectual property developed from this research could be licensed to pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology companies to turn discoveries into drugs.
Under the licensing terms, institutes agree to a 5% to 10% royalty on intellectual property developed. About 10% of all resulting revenue will go toward repaying the state bond. Once the bond is fully repaid, 100% of the revenue will return to research.
The proposition ensures that no more than 2% of all money dispersed goes to administrative expenses, keeping the bulk of state funds focused on research. However, a special carve-out provides the chosen institution additional flexibility, offering a $100 million loan for “startup costs.”
The lion’s share of the funding will be overseen by a single nonprofit research institution that is not named in the measure.
“The intent of the measure is to create in the institute a ‘hub’ of sorts for immunology and immunotherapy research, which will bring together scientists … to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures,” said Robin Swanson, spokeswoman from Yes on Prop 38.
One institute will get half the funds
Half of the $8.4 billion is earmarked for a single institution — unnamed in Proposition 38.
The measure calls for the California Department of Public Health to select “a world-class and innovative immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California.”
The recipient must meet a set of highly specific criteria, and according to CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), only one institution satisfies this threshold: the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
When asked to confirm, Proposition 38 spokeswoman Swanson acknowledged it is “very likely” CIII will be chosen.
CIII is (https://www.calimmunology.org/)a UCLA-affiliated nonprofit founded in 2024 by Dr. Gary Michelson, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken, Sean Parker and other biotech billionaires.
Notably, the proposition’s primary future beneficiaries are funding the campaign.
Campaign finance records show that of the more than $38 million raised by the “Yes on 38” campaign, the vast majority has come from Michelson and Luskin, including a $14 million loan from Michelson to his own nonprofit organization supporting the measure.

Updated October 28, 2026
Proposition 38 on the 2026 California ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) will provide vitally needed funding to cure and prevent devastating diseases that impact millions of Californians, including cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's (https://yeson38.com/faq/).
Key reasons to vote YES on Prop 38, the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative:
Helps offset federal cuts to medical research
Prop 38 responds to federal funding cuts and uncertainty (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) that are delaying life-saving medical research.
Dedicated funding for cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease research
Half of all funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) are dedicated specifically to research into cures for Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease.
Fosters collaboration between leading scientists and physicians
Grants are overseen by an Advisory Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Mandates strong accountability and transparency
State administrative costs are limited to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), with public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Designed to pay for itself – including interest
Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest.
Requires 20% discount on treatments and cures for Californians
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) below the national average.

That may include University of California campuses, such as UCLA, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UC San Francisco, UC Irvine, UC Davis, and UC Riverside; private non-profit universities, such as Stanford, USC and Caltech; and non-profit research institutions such as City of Hope, Cedars-Sinai, and Sanford Burnham Prebys, among others.
No funds from Prop 38 can be awarded to pharmaceutical companies or other for-profit corporations. (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

Proposition 38 Title and Summary | Official ... - California https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2012/general/propositions/38/title-summary.htm # California General Election ## TAX TO FUND EDUCATION AND EARLY CHILDHOOD PROGRAMS. INITIATIVE STATUTE. - Increases personal income tax rates on annual earnings over $7,316 using sliding scale from .4% for lowest individual earners to 2.2% for individuals earning over $2.5 million, for twelve years. - During first four years, allocates 60% of revenues to K–12 schools, 30% to repaying state debt, and 10% to early childhood programs. Thereafter, allocates 85% of revenues to K–12 schools, 15% to early childhood programs. - Provides K–12 funds on school-specific, per-pupil basis, subject to local control, audits, and public input. - Prohibits state from directing new funds. ### Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact: - Increase in state personal income tax revenues from 2013 through 2024. The increase would be roughly $10 billion in 2013–14, tending to increase over time. The 2012–13 increase would be about half this amount. - In each of the initial years, about $6 billion would be used for schools, $1 billion for child care and preschool, and $3 billion for state savings on debt payments. PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

Appropriates money from General Fund to repay bonds; General Fund receives 10% of licensing royalties until bonds are repaid.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the medical research bond. The state could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades if the funded research leads to discoveries that generate revenue.

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.

PROPOSED LAW
California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
“California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative.”
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
The people of the State of California find and declare all
of the following:
(a) Medical research is on the brink of achieving
transformative breakthroughs in preventing, treating,
and curing some of the most deadly and debilitating
diseases and other health disorders that afflict many
people and their loved ones every day.
(b) The emerging medical research fields of
immunology and immunotherapy offer the promise of
groundbreaking advancements in health science that,
if adequately funded, will lead to an explosion of
scientific progress in treating and preventing a wide
array of the most common medical conditions that kill
and disable Americans year after year.
(c) Immunology and immunotherapy harness the
body’s own immune system to recognize and stop
diseases. In recent years, immunotherapy has proven
to be an effective treatment in fighting cancers like
melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and
lymphomas, and more.
(d) Many doctors and research scientists believe
immunotherapies have the potential to prevent and
cure a whole range of diseases and other health
37
conditions in our lifetime, including cancer, heart
disease, neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s
and Parkinson’s, diabetes, obesity, high blood
pressure, high cholesterol, ALS (Lou Gehrig’s Disease),
HIV/AIDS, muscular dystrophy, and autoimmune
diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and
multiple sclerosis.
38
(e) Given that breakthroughs in immunology can
prevent disease and save lives, supporting immunology
and immunotherapy medical research is a vital priority
in the state’s overall approach to improving public
health and saving and improving lives.
(f) In order to fully develop and take advantage of
these emerging technologies, it is critical that a steady
and reliable source of funding be created so that
sustained research can be pursued uninterrupted by
funding shortages that would otherwise threaten to
disrupt progress and stall the momentum of scientific
breakthroughs.
(g) Public funding of medical research has always
been a central component of advancements in modern
medicine. Of all the new drugs approved by the FDA
between 2010 and 2019, the vast majority of them—
99.4 percent—were the result of publicly funded
research.
(h) California has always been at the forefront of
technological developments and breakthroughs. In
particular, California has long been a leader in the
health sciences, as it is home to many of the most
innovative and prestigious medical research institutes
in the world, as well as having the premier system of
higher education in the country—the University of
California—which houses several world-class medical
schools and health science research centers.
(i) It is incumbent on California to lead the way in the
development of immunotherapies that will yield

enormous benefits in the treatment and prevention of

(j) Besides saving lives, funding the development of

families billions of dollars in health care costs by

(k) Immunology and immunotherapy will help expand
California’s biotechnology industry, create good-paying
jobs, generate economic output, and stimulate new

Biotechnology in California has the potential to become

(l) Millions of families are hurt every year when
devastating diseases like cancer, heart disease,
Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and diabetes ruin or take the

(m) This is a pivotal moment in the history of medical
science, and California must seize the opportunity to

SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
It is the intent of the people of the State of California in
enacting this act to achieve all of the following:
(a) Fund a world-class and innovative immunology and
immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the
University of California to harness the power of the
human immune system, cutting-edge science and
technologies, and advanced computing technologies to
create scientific discoveries and next-generation
therapies for the prevention and cure of chronic
diseases, enabling Californians to live longer and
healthier lives.
(b) Award grants only to California-based public and
nonprofit universities and nonprofit medical research
institutions for immunology and immunotherapy
research and expand access to lifesaving therapies and
cures for all Californians, ensuring that no funds are
awarded to for-profit organizations or pharmaceutical
companies.
(c) Fund research, education, and the development of
treatments and therapies for various medical
conditions using immunology-based approaches at
public and nonprofit universities and other nonprofit
medical research facilities with proven track records of
conducting successful research and clinical trials, in
order to help end diseases and other illnesses like
cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s,
diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, and high
cholesterol in our lifetime.
(d) Dedicate over four billion dollars ($4,000,000,000)
specifically for research related to the prevention,
treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and
Alzheimer’s disease.
(e) Bring together biomedical scientists, disease
modelers, genomic technologists, data scientists,
computational experts, inventors of therapeutics, and
clinical trial innovators from around the globe to
develop preventative vaccines to protect against these
diseases and to formulate treatments and cures for
some of the world’s most chronic and serious medical
conditions.
(f) Select for funding a nonprofit research institute that
is independent, collaborative, and innovative, while still
affiliated with the University of California, in order to
streamline state oversight, cut through bureaucracy
and red tape, and ensure focused, outcome-driven
research.
(g) Fund a nonprofit medical research center that will
ultimately be self-sustaining by reinvesting economic
returns from successful therapeutic development into
new avenues of investigation, thereby creating a
financially independent research facility that will
eventually require no public funding.
(h) Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the

average, ensuring that Californians benefit directly

(j) Ensure that all research funding disbursed under
this act is subject to strict accountability and
transparency requirements, including a requirement
that 98 percent of all funds be spent for costs related to
medical research and development of cures, a limit on
state government administrative spending to no more
than 2 percent, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public
disclosure of all spending, and independent financial
audits.
(k) Protect and benefit the state budget by funding
research that will significantly lower health care costs
in the future and by providing opportunities for the
state to benefit from revenue resulting from patents
and licensing fees arising from immunology
breakthroughs.
(l) Benefit the California economy by creating high-
paying jobs, biomedical industrial projects, and
potential therapies that will generate new tax revenues
in our state.
(m) Raise the biotechnology and life sciences
industries in California to the status of world leadership
in the emerging field of immunotherapy research and
treatment, strengthening the state’s position as a
global hub for health innovation and economic growth.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)

In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.

Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.

Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.

The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.
How do you weigh the financial risk against the potential human cost of delaying this research?

In about a week, Californians will be casting their ballots, and among the many initiatives is Proposition 38, which seeks to raise a lot of money for medical research. But beyond the measure itself, there is the broader political question of how the initiative process is being used to support private interests.
Proposition 38, if approved, would sell $8.4 billion in state bonds to raise funding specifically for immunology and immunotherapy research. It specifies that half the funding goes toward cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.
"And immunotherapies are the cutting-edge form of medical treatment that harness the body's own immune system to stop these diseases," said Yes on 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. "And so, this bond measure steps in and provides funding for this critical medical research, which is really important right now in the face of federal cuts."
That's the interest of Dr. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist who made his fortune inventing hundreds of surgical devices. But now he's interested in creating something new: a research facility at the former Westside Pavilion shopping mall near the University of California, Los Angeles, called the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
"It's the intention of this institute to have an internal, self-funded incubator accelerator to play 'Shark Tank,' if you will. We're going to have the world's leading immunologists and say, 'Yeah, let's invest in that and start a new company,'" Michelson said at a 2024 symposium about the institute which, at that point, existed only on paper.
"Right now, we are in the phase where we are raising funds," he said. "And philanthropy is one source of that. I really would like to find some business partners."
But it seems those business partners may now be the California taxpayers. Michelson's foundation has funded the campaign to the tune of about $40 million to get Prop. 38 on the ballot. And in the measure's language, it dedicates half the money - $4.2 billion - to a single "unnamed" non-profit. But the criteria for selecting that non-profit was written to exactly match Michelson's new institute, so no other entity in the state could possibly qualify.
Dr. Sarah Hill, political science professor at California State University, Fullerton, analyzes the state's voter initiatives and says bond money is usually reserved for long-lasting infrastructure projects because it incurs debt that lasts for decades.
"And it's bond money being used for research, which is kind of unusual," said Hill. "So, it's unusual policy, and you get this kind of unusual outcome as well, of one non-profit being eligible for half the money."
The other half of the money would be handed out in a traditional, competitive process for those applying for grants to study specific projects. But that wouldn't be the case for the CIII, which critics say would also be exempt from California's public disclosure laws. Servicing the bond debt is expected to take $500-600 million from the state's general fund for 20 years or more.
Dr. Robert Kaplan, a research senior scholar at Stanford University, is concerned that lawmakers will be reluctant to fund any other kinds of medical research when so much is going to only one field of study.
"One of the important things about science is that you need a lot of different people with different ideas," said Kaplan, who authored the opposition statement to the initiative. "And so, there's kind of a marketplace for ideas, where the best minds are competing with one another to get the research funding. And then, they're evaluated on their progress and only those who succeed are rewarded with continuing funding. And that model, there seems to be a lot of discussion in the scientific literature, but that model seems to be the best one."
Ulimately, Prop. 38 will be decided by the voters on the issue of curing disease, but it also may be ushering in a whole new way for those with big ideas and enough resources to use the ballot box to convince the public to pay to make them come true.
"And I think it just raises so many questions about this process. That, at this point in the process, is about who has the money to get it on the ballot and to push for it," Hill said. "It's frustrating to watch."
"That's exactly what you want people to spend their money on, which is curing cancer," said Swanson. "So, we're proud to have gotten funding in that way."
Supporters of Prop 38 say it could end up costing the taxpayer nothing because 10% of any profits from medical breakthroughs would be refunded back to the state. But Kaplan said those kind of monetary benefits are not guaranteed and usually take decades to be realized.
